parsed.title: End-to-End Learning for Autonomous Driving: Approaches and Simulation Platforms
outline: Introduction to End-to-End Learning in Autonomous Driving
Comparison of CNN and RNN Architectures
Role of Mid-Level Representations and Simulation Environments
parsed.markdown:
End-to-end learning approaches for autonomous driving involve training models that directly map sensor inputs to control commands. Bojarski et al. [1] present a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the entire processing pipeline to steer an automobile, generating steering commands from a single front-facing center camera image. Dosovitskiy et al. [2] introduce CARLA, an open urban driving simulator used to study multiple autonomous driving approaches including end-to-end imitation learning, supporting training, prototyping, and validation of models encompassing perception and control.

Bansal et al. [3] propose ChauffeurNet, a recurrent neural network (RNN) that takes mid-level input representations and outputs driving trajectories for control. This model includes components such as FeatureNet and AgentRNN, with recurrent feedback mechanisms between iterations. ChauffeurNet enables training on both real and simulated data and supports closed-loop simulation testing before deployment.

Simulation platforms play a crucial role in autonomous driving research. CARLA [2] is an open-source simulator that supports development, training, and validation of autonomous urban driving systems, offering flexible sensor suite configurations and environmental conditions. It facilitates controlled scenario evaluation using specific metrics. Both ChauffeurNet [3] and CARLA [2] emphasize the use of mid-level representations and simulation environments to advance autonomous driving training and testing.

Despite these developments, there is a lack of direct empirical comparison between the end-to-end CNN approach [1] and the mid-level input/output RNN approach [3] under the same conditions or datasets. This gap highlights the need for studies evaluating the relative performance of these fundamentally different architectures in autonomous driving tasks.
